parsedVerdict.reasoning:
The module has one overall job: it is the HTTP adapter and composition root. server.ts builds the Express app, dependencies.ts wires domain objects into use cases, and routes.ts maps HTTP requests to those use cases. At the file level, that is cohesive.

routes.ts has two problems, though:
1. It repeats the same error-handling rule six times. Every handler has an identical catch block that turns any thrown error into a 400 response with `{ error: message }`. That policy should live in one place, such as shared error middleware or a helper.
2. It does not use its own abstraction consistently. Five routes go through use cases on `Dependencies` (`placeOrderUseCase`, `updateOrderStateUseCase`, `cancelOrderUseCase`, `listOrdersByStateUseCase`, `getStockLevelsUseCase`). The GET /api/orders/:orderId handler skips the use-case layer and calls `deps.orderRepository.getById` directly. It also has its own not-found→404 rule.

`Dependencies` makes that shortcut possible because it exposes the raw `catalog` and `orderRepository` next to the use cases. Also, dependencies.ts mixes sample data seeding (`catalog.addProduct`) into the wiring code. That is a smaller mixing of concerns.

The duplicated error rule and the inconsistent route-to-use-case path match the rubric's fail conditions.
